title: Dadaocheng and Dihua Street Walk: North Gate to Ningxia
excerpt: A self-guided 3 km afternoon walk from Taipei's North Gate up Dihua Street to Dadaocheng Wharf for sunset, finishing with dinner at Ningxia Night Market.
content:
This route crosses the old merchant quarter of Dadaocheng in one afternoon. It begins at the North Gate, the one city gate that still looks as it did in 1884, follows Dihua Street north past the cloth market and a famous matchmaking shrine, meets the Tamsui River at Dadaocheng Wharf as the sun goes down, and ends over dinner at Ningxia Night Market. Allow about 3 km of walking and 3 to 4 hours in total, and set off around three and a half hours before sunset.

The ground is flat the whole way, and much of Dihua Street has covered arcades, so a light shower is no reason to call it off. For the history of the district and more shops to look out for, read our Dihua Street and Dadaocheng guide first.

The Route

The walk finishes a few streets west of Zhongshan station, where most of the area's hotels are. Our guide to hotels in Zhongshan gives the nearest MRT exit for each one.

Step-By-Step

1 North Gate (Cheng'en Gate)

Start at Beimen MRT on the Green line. All three of its exits come up within a few minutes of the gate, which stands in a small plaza on its own traffic island. Completed in 1884, it is the only gate of the Qing-era walled city that was not restyled in 1966, and it spent decades boxed in by a road viaduct until that was demolished in 2016. There is nothing to pay and no way inside; look at it from the plaza and move on.

  • [optional] If you start earlier, the Railway Department Park across the road belongs to the National Taiwan Museum and occupies the former colonial railway headquarters. It opens Tuesday to Sunday, 09:30 to 17:00 (last tickets 16:30), and entry is NT$100.
  • Walk north up Yanping North Road, then turn left on Nanjing West Road to reach the bottom of Dihua Street. This leg is a little under a kilometre, about 12 minutes.

2 Yongle Market

Dihua Street Section 1 starts at Nanjing West Road, and the brick-fronted Yongle Market at No. 21 is almost the first thing on it. Bolts of cloth fill the second floor and tailors work on the third. The cloth floors shut on Sundays, and the cooked-food stalls downstairs mostly trade in the morning, so on an afternoon start you are here for the fabric rather than lunch.

3 Xiahai City God Temple

A minute further up, at No. 61, is the small temple that brings many visitors to this street. Building started in 1856 and finished in 1859, and it has never been enlarged, which is why some 600 statues share such a narrow hall. Most people come for the matchmaking god known as the Old Man Under the Moon (Yue Lao), who is said to tie a red thread between future partners. His statue was donated in 1971.

Entry is free and the temple opens from 07:00 to 19:00 every day. Anyone praying to Yue Lao for the first time buys a small offering pack at the counter, with a red thread, two lead coins and sugar; the temple's website sets out the order of prayers in English. The temples guide puts it alongside the city's other major shrines.

4 Dihua Street to Guisui Street

Carry on north along Dihua Street for about 300 metres to the junction with Guisui Street. This is the stretch to take slowly. The shophouse fronts change from plain Qing brick to Japanese-era Baroque plasterwork, and the ground floors sell dried mango, mushrooms, Chinese herbs and tea, with design shops and cafés tucked into the deep courtyards behind. Lee Huajiah, the traditional pastry shop at No. 309, is further up the street if you want to buy something to take home.

  • Older guides send readers to the Lin Liu-Hsin Puppet Theatre Museum near here. It closed in July 2019.
  • From Guisui Street, turn left and head west towards the river. Go through the floodwall at Water Gate No. 5, at the end of Minsheng West Road, to reach the wharf. Allow about 6 minutes.

5 Dadaocheng Wharf at sunset

Tea was shipped out of this river bank in the 19th century. Now there is a riverside park, a ferry pier and the PIER5 container market, a cluster of shipping containers turned into food and drink stalls with seating on the upper decks. Taipei's tourism office lists the market as open all year, from 16:00 to 22:00 on weekdays and from 12:00 to 22:00 at weekends. The river runs north to south here, so you look straight across it to the west as the sun drops.

Sunset in Taipei falls between about 17:03 in late November and early December and 18:47 in early July. In late October it is around 17:15. There is a YouBike station on the wharf if you would rather ride the riverside path afterwards.

  • Once it is dark, walk east along Minsheng West Road for roughly 900 metres, about 12 to 15 minutes, to the night market. You pass back across Dihua Street on the way.

6 Ningxia Night Market

The stalls line Ningxia Road between Minsheng West Road and Nanjing West Road, with a pedestrian lane between the food carts and the traffic. The city lists the market as open from 17:00 to 23:30 every day, although each stall keeps its own hours. Our Michelin night market guide marks the stands that have been recognised here.

Where to Eat

The route is timed for an afternoon start, so the best eating comes at the end. Some practical options along the way:

  • Before you set off: the ground floor of Yongle Market is a morning food hall. Lin He Fa, known for its sticky oil rice, trades from about 07:30 until noon or until it sells out, and closes on Mondays. Arrive for an early lunch and start the walk from there.
  • On Dihua Street: dried fruit, nuts and pork paper from the wholesalers make an easy snack while you walk, and the street's tea houses are covered in the Dadaocheng guide.
  • At the wharf: the container stalls sell drinks and light food, enough to tide you over while you wait for the sun.
  • At the finish: Ningxia Night Market is the main meal. Taro balls, pork liver soup, shredded chicken rice and oyster omelettes are its best-known dishes, and the queues are longest at the Michelin-listed stalls.

Best Time to Go

Tuesday to Saturday suits the route best. On Sundays the cloth floors at Yongle Market are shut, and on Mondays a number of Dihua shops and cafés take their day off, as does the Railway Department Park. Most of Dihua Street trades every day, though, so either day still works if it is your only chance. At weekends the container market opens at noon rather than 16:00.

Work back from sunset to choose a start time:

  • November to January: sunset is between about 17:03 and 17:40, so leave the North Gate at about 13:30.
  • February to April and September to October: sunset moves between roughly 17:15 and 18:25, so start at some point from 14:00 to 15:00, later in the lighter months.
  • May to August: sunset is between about 18:15 and 18:47, so start at about 15:00 to 15:30. Summer afternoons are hot, and the shaded arcades on Dihua Street help.

In the weeks before Lunar New Year, Dihua Street becomes the city's New Year market and is extremely crowded. The 2026 market ran from 31 January to 15 February. Dates for 2027 have not been announced yet; Lunar New Year's Eve falls on 5 February 2027, and the market normally runs for about two weeks before it.

Getting There and Back

Start: Beimen station (G13) on the Green line. Beimen is linked underground to the Airport MRT terminal at Taipei Main Station (A1), which makes the gate an easy first stop on the afternoon you arrive from Taoyuan Airport.

Finish: Shuanglian station (R12) on the Red line, about 10 minutes' walk from the market via exit 1. Zhongshan station (Red and Green lines) is about 10 minutes away via exit 5. Daqiaotou on the Orange line is the closest station to the north end of Dihua Street if you want to cut the walk short after stop 4.

You can walk the route in reverse, but the wharf is the reason for the timing, and in reverse you would reach it in the middle of the afternoon.

Common Questions

How long is the walk?

About 3 km between the six stops, or around 40 minutes of actual walking. With time in the market, the temple and the shops, plus waiting for sunset, plan on 3 to 4 hours.

Is the wharf container market open in winter?

Yes. According to Taipei's official tourism site it runs all year, from 16:00 on weekdays and from noon at weekends, closing at 22:00. Typhoons and special events can close it, and those notices go on the market's own social media.

What are the Xiahai City God Temple's opening hours?

07:00 to 19:00 daily, all year round, apart from closures for typhoons or other natural disasters. Entry is free; the offering pack for the matchmaking god is bought at the counter inside.

Can I do the walk in the morning instead?

You can, and Yongle Market's food stalls are at their best before noon. You would miss the sunset at the wharf, though, and Ningxia Night Market does not open until 17:00, so a morning walk needs a different ending.

Is the walk suitable for wheelchairs and pushchairs?

Mostly. The route is level, and the tourism office lists the wharf, the temple and Yongle Market as wheelchair accessible, and the wharf and Yongle Market also have accessible toilets.
